I'm verifying the annotation's written_attributes list message_id and reaction_type for the new reaction row, and that computation attributes correctly reference the matched message_id needed to write it. But I'm noticing the written_attributes might be missing the actual new reaction identifier itself.

Now I'm checking the selector logic against the sketch, confirming it filters for reactions of type raised_hands tied to Priya Sharma, matching messages 1 and 2 and mapping them to row bindings.

Rows 3-6 correctly test negatives - wrong reaction type, wrong person, no reactions, and mismatched pairs where different users react differently on the same message - all properly excluded since the selector requires reaction_type and real_name to bind on the same reaction node.

I'm also verifying the relationship roles across messages, message_reactions, and users join correctly on a single row, and cross-checking the referent set and near-misses against the sketch, which all line up, so now I'm moving to check for any extra unintended matches.

I check quantifiers and unrelated messages aren't accidentally near misses, confirm no ID-scope restrictions leak intended answers, and validate the operation writes reaction_type "rocket" with the actor field correctly excluded since it's supplied by auth. Everything looks consistent, and none of the message texts appear to leak the answer.

Wait, "Rocket specs draft" itself contains the word "Rocket," which could act as an unintended keyword hint toward the emoji being added — that's a real quality concern worth flagging even though the other message texts (budget review, vendor contract, timeline update, etc.) look fine.

But actually the selection criteria is based on reactions from Priya, not text content, so this is only a coincidental overlap and not a genuine leak — a weak flag at most. Overall the operation looks correctly scoped: reactions.add mapping message_id and reaction_type="rocket" onto the two messages Priya reacted to with raised_hands matches the reactions API design intent.

That naming was inherited from the original sketch design rather than introduced during compilation, so it's not a defect worth flagging - just an ordinary stylistic choice. Overall I'm marking this as valid with strong quality and no real issues.
